findings.title: Tautological article UPDATE policy permits arbitrary defacement
preconditions: The vulnerable migration is deployed and the articles table is exposed through the Supabase Data API
The anon role retains UPDATE privilege on articles and the public Supabase URL and anon key are available to the caller
At least one article exists; its UUID is obtainable through the unrestricted article SELECT path or public article links
The submitted replacement values satisfy the table's basic type, NOT NULL, and foreign-key constraints
findings.rationale:
The real browser sink updates an article selected only by route-controlled id at src/pages/ArticlePage.tsx:55-64 through the public Supabase client at src/lib/supabase.ts:6-13. The isAuthor comparison at src/pages/ArticlePage.tsx:21 is used only to hide buttons at lines 239-255 and is absent from the database request. The UPDATE policy has neither a TO restriction nor an auth.uid() ownership check and instead uses a tautology at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:76-78; the public SELECT policy at lines 68-69 also makes article identifiers discoverable. No GRANT restriction, REVOKE, trigger, protective RPC, or server-side authorization layer limits a direct Data API UPDATE by a role holding table privileges.

The tautological UPDATE policy authorizes every article row and has no authenticated-role restriction, so an unauthenticated remote caller can bypass the browser-only ownership check. Arbitrary modification of article content, publication state, and valid author references creates broad persistent integrity impact with low attack complexity and no user interaction.

findings.title: Public profile policy exposes every user's email
preconditions: None beyond access to the deployed Supabase Data API and its publicly distributed anonymous client credentials
findings.rationale:
The browser bundle constructs a Supabase client from the public URL and anon key at src/lib/supabase.ts:6-13, while the profiles table stores email at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:11-16. Its SELECT policy has no role restriction and applies USING (true) at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:43-45; no GRANT restriction, REVOKE, protective view, or server-only boundary exists in the repository. The application's concrete profiles read uses .select('*') at src/components/Profile.tsx:23-27, and its UI authentication path does not constrain a direct anonymous Data API request. The demo intent stated at README.md:1-12 does not trigger exclusion rule 3 under the supplied Supatest-specific instruction.

Any remote user can query the profiles table through the anonymous browser client because the SELECT policy applies without a role restriction and unconditionally permits every row. Since the API exposes all selected columns, this enables unauthenticated bulk disclosure of stored email addresses with no attacker-specific precondition.

findings.title: SECURITY DEFINER RPC exposes profile PII without caller authorization
preconditions: Network access to the public RPC endpoint
Knowledge or a correct guess of a registered user's exact email address
findings.rationale:
get_user_by_email is itself the Data API RPC entry point: it accepts caller-controlled email input and returns profile identifiers, usernames, emails, and avatars at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:90-99. It runs with definer privileges at line 93 but performs no auth.uid(), JWT, role, ownership, or tenant check, and the scoped source contains no REVOKE EXECUTE or restrictive grant. Assuming the standard Supabase exposure of public-schema functions, PostgreSQL's default PUBLIC execution privilege lets an anonymous caller invoke this PII oracle directly even though no frontend .rpc() call exists.

An unauthenticated remote caller can invoke the SECURITY DEFINER RPC to retrieve another user's profile PII. Requiring an exact registered email limits blind enumeration, but emails are commonly known or guessable and repeated queries can expose multiple profiles, so the confidentiality impact remains high.

findings.title: Public article policy exposes unpublished drafts

Although Home adds published = true in client code at src/components/ArticleList.tsx:35-50, a caller can bypass that convention with a direct Data API list request through the public client configured at src/lib/supabase.ts:6-13. Random UUIDs do not invoke exclusion rule 15 because unrestricted collection queries can enumerate drafts without guessing an id.

findings.title: Tautological profile UPDATE policy permits cross-user modification
preconditions: Attacker can authenticate as any ordinary application user and obtain a valid session token
Attacker can identify or address another user's profile row through the public Data API
findings.rationale:
The real browser update path calls profiles.update(...).eq('id', userId) at src/components/Profile.tsx:45-51 through the publicly configured Supabase client at src/lib/supabase.ts:6-13. The database policy has no TO restriction or auth.uid() comparison and uses the universally true predicate at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:53-55; with no separate WITH CHECK, it also supplies no ownership protection for the replacement row. The public SELECT policy at supabase/migrations/20250201000000_initial_vulnblog.sql:43-45 exposes target identifiers, and no repository GRANT restriction, REVOKE, trigger, or server-side authorization layer limits a direct Data API update by a role holding UPDATE privileges. The userId filter is attacker-controlled client behavior rather than an authorization boundary, and the Supatest-specific instruction prevents the deliberate-demo labels from invoking exclusion rule 3.

The tautological UPDATE policy permits any authenticated user to satisfy the row-level authorization check, enabling cross-user profile modification through the public Data API. Exploitation has two practical preconditions—an ordinary authenticated session and an addressable victim row—so the matrix assigns MEDIUM severity.

findings.title: Raw authentication responses may disclose registered emails
findings.rationale: Anonymous users can reach the Auth form through src/App.tsx:86-109, and attacker-controlled emails reach both signInWithPassword and signUp at src/components/Auth.tsx:17-38. The component renders the resulting provider Error.message at src/components/Auth.tsx:57-60, but that is exploitable for enumeration only if the configured Supabase project returns observably different outcomes for registered and unregistered addresses. The repository records only the project URL and anon key placeholders at .env.example:4-5 and contains no auth configuration or measured provider responses, so static evidence cannot establish the required distinction. Raw error forwarding is risky behavior, but without proof of distinguishable responses this remains missing hardening rather than a demonstrated enumeration oracle.
